title: Two's complement (signed integer representation)
summary: Two's complement is the standard representation for signed integers. An n-bit two's complement number: the most significant bit is the sign bit (0 = non-negative, 1 = negative). Negative value of x = (2^n - x) = invert all bits of x and add 1. Range: -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1. Addition and subtraction use the same hardware as unsigned (overflow wraps).

Negative value of x = (2^n - x) = invert all bits of x and add 1. Range: -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1. Addition and subtraction use the same hardware as unsigned (overflow wraps).

structure.meaning: For non-negative: the value. For negative: 2^n - |value|.
Negate x: ~x + 1 (invert all bits, add 1). Or: 2^n - x.
Only one representation of zero (all zeros). (Unlike sign-magnitude which has +0 and -0.)
Overflow occurs when the result exceeds the range. Detected by: sign of operands same, sign of result different.

notes: Two's complement is used by all modern CPUs (x86, ARM, RISC-V).
Addition and subtraction use the same circuitry as unsigned (modular arithmetic).
Multiplication requires sign extension (Booth's algorithm or similar).
Two's complement simplifies hardware: no separate subtraction circuit needed.
The name 'two's complement' comes from the operation: complement (invert) then add 2 (i.e., +1 to the one's complement).
